title: When to Start BLW: Baby-Led Weaning Age Chart + Stages | Hacé Cuentas
h1: When to Start BLW: Age & Stage Calculator
description: Enter your baby's age in months to find out if they're ready for baby-led weaning, which BLW stage they're in, and what foods to offer.
answerSnippet: Baby-led weaning (BLW) can start at **6 months** when the baby can sit with minimal support, holds their head up steadily, and shows interest in food. Before 6 months, breast milk or formula provides 100% of nutrition. Stages: 6–8 months = Intro (soft strips); 9–11 months = Growing variety; 12+ months = Family food without added salt or sugar.
intro: Baby-Led Weaning (BLW) is a feeding approach where infants self-feed soft, appropriately sized solid foods instead of being spoon-fed purees. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), CDC, and WHO, solid foods should not be introduced before **4 months**, and most babies are developmentally ready at **6 months** when three readiness signs are present: sitting with minimal support, stable head control, and demonstrated interest in food. This calculator evaluates your baby's age in months against WHO/CDC/AAP developmental benchmarks to determine BLW readiness, the appropriate introduction stage, and safe food textures for that stage.
keyTakeaway: **BLW readiness = Age ≥ 6 months AND upright sitting AND head control AND interest in food.** All 3 developmental signs must be present — age alone is not enough. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months before any solid food introduction.
useCases: A parent with a 5.5-month-old who is sitting up early wants to know if early BLW introduction is safe before the WHO 6-month mark.
A caregiver of a 7-month-old baby who still shows tongue-thrust reflex needs guidance on whether to wait longer before offering soft solids.
A pediatrician counseling a family on progressing from Stage 1 (single-ingredient soft strips) to Stage 2 (mixed textures and finger foods) around 8–9 months.
Parents of a 10-month-old ready to transition to Stage 3 BLW foods — small soft pieces, family meals, and self-feeding with pincer grasp — want a structured reference chart.
A nutrition-conscious family following WHO/USDA Dietary Guidelines wants to know which allergen foods (peanuts, eggs, fish) to introduce early during BLW and at what age.
A daycare provider tracking multiple infants across different BLW stages needs a quick age-to-stage reference to ensure appropriate food textures and choking-safe preparation.

explanation:
## When to Start BLW: The 6-Month Rule

The WHO, AAP, and CDC align on a clear threshold: complementary foods — including Baby-Led Weaning — should begin at **6 months (26 weeks of corrected age)**, never before 4 months. Before that point, the infant's gut lacks sufficient digestive enzymes, the intestinal barrier is still "open" (permeable to large proteins), and the swallow-breathe coordination needed to handle solids safely is not yet mature. Starting too early is associated with increased risk of obesity, allergies, and respiratory aspiration.

> **Important:** For premature babies, use **corrected age** (gestational age at birth + weeks since birth), not chronological age. A baby born at 34 weeks who is now 10 weeks old has a corrected age of only ~6 weeks — nowhere near ready for solids.

---

## How This Calculator Works

The tool evaluates two inputs:

1. **Baby's age in weeks** — calculated from date of birth to today.
2. **Readiness checklist** — three developmental milestones that must ALL be present simultaneously.

Age alone is not sufficient. A baby can be 26 weeks old and still not meet the physical readiness criteria. Conversely, no checklist can override the 4-month minimum; developmental signs before 17 weeks are **never** grounds to start solids.

The calculator outputs the current stage (see chart below) and indicates whether starting BLW is recommended, not yet recommended, or approaching the window.

---

## The Three Readiness Signs (All Three Required)

1. **Head control:** Holds head erect and steady without support for several seconds. If the head still wobbles, the airway cannot be protected adequately during eating.
2. **Supported sitting:** Sits upright with minimal support — in a lap or slightly reclined high chair — with trunk reasonably stable. Full independent sitting is *not* required, but slumping or flopping is a disqualifier.
3. **Interest in food:** Watches others eat, reaches toward food or plates, opens mouth when food approaches. The loss of the tongue-thrust reflex (which automatically pushes foreign objects out of the mouth) is part of this same developmental window.

The **tongue-thrust reflex** typically fades between 4 and 6 months. Its persistence after 6 months is uncommon but warrants a pediatric assessment before proceeding with BLW.

---

## BLW Stage Chart by Age

| Age | BLW Ready? | Stage | Typical Foods | Format |
|-----|-----------|-------|---------------|--------|
| < 6 months | ❌ No | Exclusive milk | Breast milk or formula only | — |
| 6–8 months | ✅ Yes | BLW Start | Avocado, banana, sweet potato, squash | Long soft strips (~7–8 cm) |
| 9–11 months | ✅ Yes | Growing variety | Shredded meat, soft legumes, fruit chunks | Small pieces (~1 cm, pincer grasp) |
| ≥ 12 months | ✅ Yes | Varied family food | Family meals, no added salt or sugar | Family-sized portions |

---

## Recommended Foods by Stage

**Stage 1 — Start (6–8 months):** Foods must be soft enough to squash between two adult fingers with light pressure — this is the standard safety test. Format: long strips (roughly the length of an adult finger) so the baby can grip with a **palmar grasp** and gnaw from the top. The portion sticking out above the fist is what gets eaten; the rest is the "handle."

Examples: avocado strips, peeled ripe banana, steamed sweet potato, cooked butternut squash, soft ripe pear (peeled), steamed broccoli florets (the floret acts as a natural handle).

**Stage 2 — Growing variety (9–11 months):** The emerging **pincer grasp** (thumb + index finger) allows smaller pieces. Introduce animal proteins: shredded chicken or turkey, ground beef or lamb, flaked cooked fish (boneless), soft scrambled egg. Add cooked legumes (lentils, black beans), soft pasta shapes, and small pieces of ripe fruit. Iron-rich foods become especially important here — breast milk alone no longer meets iron needs after ~6 months.

**Stage 3 — Family food (12 months+):** The baby joins family meals with texture and variety, avoiding added salt, added sugar, honey (botulism risk under 12 months), whole cow's milk as a main drink (under 12 months), and hard/round choking hazards (whole grapes, whole nuts, large raw carrot pieces, whole cherry tomatoes).

---

## What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- **Allergy guidance:** Early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut, egg, tree nuts) is now recommended by the AAP *around* 6 months for most infants — but the timing and method depend on eczema severity and family history. This calculator does not replace an allergist or pediatrician consultation for high-risk babies.
- **Medical conditions:** Babies with neuromuscular disorders, cleft palate, Down syndrome, or severe reflux require individualized feeding plans beyond what any general calculator can provide.
- **Milk intake tracking:** BLW does not replace milk feeds. Breast milk or formula remains the **primary nutrition source** until 12 months; solids are complementary, not a substitute.

---

## Common Errors to Avoid

| Error | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|
| Starting at 4 months because "the baby seemed interested" | Interest alone is not readiness; the gut and airway are not mature |
| Using chronological age for a premature baby | Can lead to starting weeks too early; always use corrected age |
| Offering round, firm, or coin-shaped foods | Top choking hazards: whole grapes, hot dog rounds, hard raw vegetables |
| Skipping the finger-squash test | Texture is more predictive of choking risk than food type |
| Stopping milk feeds too early | Solid food cannot replicate breast milk or formula's nutritional density under 12 months |

---

*Always confirm the timing and approach with your baby's pediatrician, especially if there is any history of premature birth, feeding difficulties, or suspected allergy risk.*

faq.q: At exactly what age can I start Baby-Led Weaning?
faq.a: The CDC, WHO, and AAP all agree: **no earlier than 6 months** (26 weeks). Before this age, the infant digestive and neuromuscular systems are not mature enough for solid foods. Starting too early increases risks of choking, allergies, and overfeeding. Age 6 months is the minimum threshold — and only if the other three developmental readiness signs are also present.

faq.q: What are the 3 signs of BLW readiness?
faq.a: According to the AAP, the three simultaneous readiness signs are: (1) sitting upright with minimal support (not just propped), with stable head and neck control; (2) loss of the tongue-thrust reflex (baby doesn't automatically push food out with tongue); and (3) demonstrated interest in food — reaching for it or watching others eat intently. All three must be present, not just one or two.

faq.q: Is BLW safe? What about choking risk?
faq.a: Research published in *Pediatrics* (Fangupo et al., 2016) found no significant difference in choking incidents between BLW and traditional spoon-feeding when foods are prepared correctly. Key safety rules: food must be soft enough to mash between your fingers, never round and firm, and babies must always be supervised and seated upright. Gagging (a normal reflex) is very different from choking and is actually part of how babies learn to manage food in their mouth.

faq.q: What foods should I introduce first in BLW Stage 1?
faq.a: Best first BLW foods at 6 months are soft, easy-to-grip strips about 2–3 inches long: steamed broccoli florets, avocado spears, ripe banana, cooked sweet potato sticks, and soft-cooked zucchini. The USDA recommends iron-rich foods early (iron-fortified cereals, pureed meats, cooked lentils) since breast milk iron decreases after 6 months and infant iron stores deplete. Introduce one new food every 3–5 days.

faq.q: When should I introduce allergenic foods like peanuts, eggs, and fish?
faq.a: The AAP's updated guidelines (based on the LEAP and EAT studies) recommend introducing common allergens — peanuts, eggs, tree nuts, fish, wheat, soy, sesame — around **6 months**, not delaying until after age 1. For high-risk infants (eczema or egg allergy), consult a pediatrician first. For low-risk infants, early introduction at home is encouraged. Offer allergens consistently: 2–3 times per week after the first successful exposure.

faq.q: Can I do BLW if I'm formula-feeding instead of breastfeeding?
faq.a: Yes — BLW is equally appropriate for formula-fed and breastfed babies. The feeding method before solids does not affect BLW suitability. What matters is developmental readiness at 6 months. Formula-fed babies should continue receiving **at least 24–32 oz of formula per day** during Stage 1 and Stage 2 BLW, as solids at this stage are supplemental, not a replacement, per AAP guidelines.

faq.q: What foods are absolutely off-limits in the first year?
faq.a: The CDC and AAP list the following as prohibited under 12 months: **honey** (botulism risk from *Clostridium botulinum* spores), **cow's milk as a main drink** (okay in cooking/yogurt), **added salt**, **added sugar**, **unpasteurized foods**, **high-mercury fish** (shark, swordfish, tilefish, king mackerel), and all **choking hazard foods** (whole grapes, whole nuts, raw carrots, popcorn, large chunks of cheese or meat). These restrictions apply regardless of feeding method.

faq.q: How much should my baby eat during BLW Stage 1?
faq.a: Very little — and that's completely normal. In Stage 1 (6–8 months), most food ends up on the floor, tray, or bib. The WHO and AAP emphasize that **breast milk or formula remains the primary nutrition source until 12 months**. Offer solids 1–2 times per day in small amounts (a few strips or pieces), and never pressure the baby to eat more. Appetite self-regulation is one of BLW's key documented benefits per *JAMA Pediatrics* (Townsend & Pitchford, 2012).

faq.q: What's the difference between BLW and traditional puree feeding?
faq.a: With purees (traditional method), the adult decides how much the baby eats and spoon-feeds; the baby doesn't control the pace. With BLW, the baby self-regulates, touches, smells, and explores food at their own pace. Studies published in *Appetite* and *BMJ Open* suggest children raised with BLW show better appetite regulation and lower tendency toward overweight at age 5, though both methods are safe and valid.

faq.q: Can I mix BLW with purees?
faq.a: Yes. The mixed approach — offering both strips/pieces and purees or spoon-feeding — is valid and accepted. Some specialists call it 'modified BLW' or BLISS (Baby-Led Introduction to SolidS). There is no evidence that mixing both approaches is harmful. What matters is that the baby has the opportunity to practice self-feeding and explore textures.
